The Importance of CSR in Businesses Today
The Importance of CSR in Businesses Today - Essay Example - ThesisArcPro
This essay examines why corporate social responsibility matters, covering its impact on brand reputation, talent retention, and business growth.
Business and management writer, 5+ yrs experience

CSR is one of the key business practices that engages the community and corporate entities. In the current corporate space, CSR is shaping business, and most entities are adopting the strategy in making ethical decisions about business progress and expansion. CSR offers diverse tangible advantages that strengthen companies' financial strength, talent pool, reputation and also engages the society to expand the market and build a positive business environment. In the current era, the approach is becoming a competitive advantage to most companies because they use the strategy to manage their operations, understanding the market and positively strengthening their ability to safeguard the environment, reduce climate change and use available resources to prioritize the safety of the customers and maximizing the advantages of the business to society. This essay focuses on the benefits of CSR to businesses.

<!--split-->
**Builds Brand Reputation**

CSR allows companies to build their reputation by supporting a commitment to social and environmental aspects. One advantage of creating a reputation is that companies can influence how consumers make their purchases, positively affect consumer behaviour and their perception about brands and the advantages of the products to society and the environment (Wirba, 2024). When the competitive advantages of the products are influenced by the reputation and branding based on CSR programs, the company leverages the market and becomes stronger in the long run. Most successful companies have adopted CSR programs to engage the community and have a positive relationship with the market. When the market environment is welcoming to the companies' brands, it becomes easy to succeed in the competitive environment. Brand reputation is a key strategy that encourages companies to focus on growth, ensure sustainability and achieve their targeted business objectives.

**Attracts and Retains Top Talent**

Employees in the current corporate space also weigh companies beyond the benefits they gain from them. Currently, workers are also examining whether companies are interested in promoting values and abilities that support social and community projects. The ability to support such projects allows companies to have a positive relationship with society and boost morale for interactions and the acceptability of the products (Wickert, 2021). Stronger CSR programs enable companies to have stronger business performance, increase business commitment to addressing complex issues that affect operations, and develop competence in a changing corporate environment. When workers are satisfied with their workplace environment, they increase their productivity, lower turnover issues and experience job satisfaction. Retaining talent reduces the costs of recruitment and finding competent skills in the future.

**Improves Financial Performance**

CSR increases the financial advantages of the company in the industry. Studies show that companies practicing CSR attract stakeholders to support the companies financially. Visible investment in companies with CSR programs ensures that they make investments in firms that have advantages to the community and the entire society (Quezado et al., 2022). Financial investment expands the company, allowing it to grow, become competent and cope with market dynamics in ways that increase its ability to grow and expand its product value and sustainability.

**Mitigates Risk**

CSR assists most companies in overcoming risks in the market. Escaping such risks allows the company to work in a positive workplace environment and avoid legal and ethical issues during production. When markets experience political changes, most companies become vulnerable to changes including sustainability and taxation. Using CSR engages environmental protection and carbon credit measures which support positive interactions between businesses and political entities (Ahsan, 2024). This is especially valuable in large projects, allowing companies to grow, work positively and influence their operations favorably to achieve their future business targets.

<!--split-->

**Drives Innovation and Competitiveness**

CSR boosts innovation and ensures competitiveness. Embracing CSR ensures that companies embrace innovation and technology to promote carbon reduction, increase environmental safety, and focus on building a positive relationship with the community. When the community has a positive relationship with the business, companies create leverage to foster growth, ensure sustainability, and create an environment that facilitates growth in the future (Ahsan, 2024). Especially in a competitive environment, companies have to differentiate their products to remain competent and able to handle risks involved in the market.

**Promotes Environmental Sustainability**

CSR promotes environmental protection. In an era where emissions are threatening to increase climate change, there is a need to initiate programs to protect the planet from emissions and other risks. Emissions are becoming an imminent problem that limits companies' ability to secure the ecosystem's safety and well-being (Vuong & Bui, 2023). Companies that adhere to environmental protection have higher advantages of cushioning the ecosystem from the risks of emissions, which might have negative implications on performance, value and ability to grow in the long run.

**Upholds Ethical Practices**

Ethics in business is vital in shaping operations, behavior and employee perception. Companies use such advantages to attract clients from different parts of the world because of respecting the environment, designing engagement programs with the community, and prioritizing the safety of the planet rather than using unethical practices to earn profits (Vuong & Bui, 2023). Reducing emissions and using the right methods, including waste management and compliance with carbon credits, increases ethical production and also encourages new players in the market to adopt the same. Businesses thrive because of ethics and working competitively under established regulations.

In conclusion, businesses use CSR programs to prioritize the environment, the community and having a positive relationship with society. Using CSR programs increases the value of the environment, strengthens brands and positively influences consumer behavior to prioritize sustainability and protection of the ecosystem to achieve better business practices in the future. Even in a competitive environment, CSR reduces legal issues and inconveniences that can affect operations, performance and value of companies in the long run. While companies are struggling to integrate CSR into their growth programs, it is a program that boosts financial and operational performance, increases investment and creates value for companies in the changing business environment.

Nursing Ethics Essay: Dilemmas in Practice
Nursing Ethics Essay: Dilemmas in Practice - Essay Example - ThesisArcPro
This nursing ethics essay examines real dilemmas nurses face daily, exploring autonomy, confidentiality, end-of-life care, and ethical frameworks in practice.

Nurses make dozens of decisions during every shift, some of which are moral ones that are more than just a checklist or chart. She is not just doing her job when she's asked to sedate an aggressive patient, when someone she's asked to restrain can't do it on their own, or when she has to soften the blow of a terminal diagnosis for a grieving family. She is deciding between two competing goods and, at times, even two competing bad outcomes. This is a moral dilemma at its core: a choice that conflicts with another moral choice. Such problems seldom present themselves overtly or explicitly, and sometimes nurses only become aware in retrospect which principle they emphasized and which they set aside. The tension between patient autonomy, beneficence, justice, and confidentiality and the realities of law, resources, and institutional structure creates ethical challenges in nursing practice. It is vital to grasp these dilemmas and the frameworks nurses employ in their decision-making to preserve patient care and the ethical standards of nursing practice.

Nursing is a unique career in health care. Nurses spend more continuous time at the bedside than any other clinical profession, but often lack the formal authority over treatment decisions as compared to physicians. This proximity and power imbalance enables an ethical landscape to emerge. A nurse can see that a patient may be suffering unnecessarily for their wishes to be realized, or that the wishes are being disregarded before anyone else can. However, she might not have the position she needs to alter the plan. This conflict is expressed directly by Duarte et al. (2023), who stated that Brazilian nursing laws are sometimes not aligned with practice, placing nurses at legal risk if they have to act based on knowledge and skills that are not yet regulated by law. This inequity is not exclusive to Brazil and is found wherever the scope of nursing practice grows more quickly than the enabling legislation or hospital policies for nursing. The four principles of nursing ethics are autonomy (respecting patients' decisions), beneficence (doing what is good for the patient), nonmaleficence (avoiding causing harm to the patient), and justice (caring for patients fairly). All problems that nurses encounter are ultimately a struggle between these four commitments.

The dilemma of patient autonomy versus medical paternalism is probably the most widely known. A nurse can be placed in a difficult situation where she is required to accept a treatment that she feels is lifesaving, while a competent adult has refused it, due to her duty to respect people's decisions and her instinct to promote health. A version of this conflict was recorded by Caro-Alonso et al. (2023) during the COVID-19 pandemic, when nurses in Spain physically restrained patients with intellectual disabilities to prevent them from leaving COVID-19 isolation rooms. Nurses who were interviewed talked about this being the breaking of the autonomy of individuals for the well-being of the community, and they knew it.

<!--split-->

The issue of confidentiality is another challenge. Whilst patient confidentiality is always the responsibility of the nurse, there are situations where disclosure to a family member, a partner, or a public health authority may be required in order to prevent harm. Whether the duty to warn outweighs the duty to protect privacy is a judgment that is not fully prepared for by any policy manual.

One type of care that presents some of the most emotionally challenging situations that nurses may face is end-of-life care. When it comes to do-not-resuscitate orders, withdrawal of life support, and differing opinions among family members about a patient's wishes, nurses become central decision makers in choices they didn't choose to make. The study by Caro-Alonso et al. (2023) revealed that nurses sometimes reduced the information they shared when contacted by phone to inform relatives of the death of a patient with COVID-19. This situation did not leave them feeling comfortable with the lack of honesty.

Dilemmas of resource allocation and short-staffing also arise. In situations where beds, ventilators, or staff time are limited, nurses have to make decisions, either through their actions or words, about who gets care first. The same study found that age was sometimes used as a triage method adopted early in the pandemic, reserving care for younger patients. Nurses commented that they saw the principle of justice being violated because of events beyond their sphere of influence.

Issues of informed consent are also complicated, especially where language barriers, cognitive impairment, or reduced capacity due to age or illness exist. An additional layer to this is that newly licensed nurses and nursing students might be hesitant to challenge more experienced nurses when they feel that something is not right, according to Hwu and Pai (2025). This matters because it influences what nurses tell patients, as well as what they believe they can speak out for on the patient's behalf. This hierarchy adds to the complexity of the consent and disclosure process.

A Nursing Leadership Essay: Comparing Key Styles
A Nursing Leadership Essay: Comparing Key Styles - Essay Example - ThesisArcPro
This nursing leadership essay compares transformational, transactional, autocratic, and servant styles used across modern healthcare settings.

The actions of nursing leaders directly impact patient safety, staff morale and the quality of patient care provided in health care delivery systems. Nurse leaders are being asked to navigate a range of complex conditions, including a lack of staff, changing clinical needs, and high pressure, in their work with varied teams. There is no one-size-fits-all leadership style that is applicable to all situations nurse leaders face. Rather, there are multiple styles, such as transformational, transactional, autocratic and servant leadership, which provide nurse leaders with a variety of tools to address a specific clinical context. This essay will discuss the four leadership styles and their main attributes, advantages and disadvantages in the context of nursing. It suggests that successful nurse leaders are not always a specific type of leader, but are flexible with their style based on the clinical situation they face.

<!--split-->

Transformational leadership is about inspiring and motivating employees to achieve a shared vision of the future by providing mentoring and caring for employees as a means of supporting individual growth. The nurse leader embraces innovation, sets a good example for ethical behavior, and invests in the professional growth of staff. In their systematic review, Niinihuhta and Häggman-Laitila (2022) found that transformational leadership showed the highest positive correlations with measurable aspects of the wellbeing of nurses compared to all other styles they examined, including authentic, resonant and servant. Similarly, Alluhaybi et al. (2023) identified transformational behaviours as being closely associated with increased staff work engagement, such as increased dedication and vigor, amongst their sample of nurses from a variety of healthcare environments.

The benefits of transformational leadership are widely known. It helps to reduce burnout, increases trust, and creates an atmosphere of appreciation instead of management. But this style also has its drawbacks. Transformational leadership requires building relationships and trust, and this takes time, leading to less immediate applicability in emergencies or acute crises. It also demands strong interpersonal and communication skills, a trait some nurse leaders do not have. A nurse manager leading a unit through a major change is likely to need to exercise transformational leadership to gain staff buy-in. At the same time, a sudden surge of patients would require another level of leadership.

<!--split-->

Transactional leadership is based on a set of clearly defined expectations, a clear system of supervision, and a system of rewards or corrective action based on performance. This style focuses on efficiency, consistency and accountability, not on emotional attachment and long-term vision. According to Moreira et al. (2026), the second most frequent leadership style among Portuguese nurses was the transactional style, and the two styles were positively related, implying that transactional behaviors are not necessarily in conflict with transformational leadership, but are in fact often used in conjunction with it. Their study revealed that the most powerful aspect of transactional leadership among the nurses studied was contingent reward, which involves acknowledging and rewarding good performance.

The positive aspect of transactional leadership is its application in achieving regulatory requirements and standardization of clinical protocols. This structured process is useful for tasks like medication administration routines, shift assignments and compliance audits. But there are real drawbacks to transactional leadership. If used too strictly, it can stifle creativity and lower nurses' sense of autonomy, and it doesn't do much to foster long-term commitment the way transformational leadership does. Most effective nurse leaders combine transactional and more relational approaches to leadership rather than relying on the former for everyday management of activities.

Autocratic leadership involves decision-making at the top, with the leader assuming most or all authority and little opportunity for input from employees. This style is not collaborative, but emphasizes quickness and decisiveness. Al Thawabiya et al. (2023) conducted a study on nurse leaders in Qatar that revealed that directors of nursing generally displayed transformational leadership qualities. Still, the head nurses who were closer to the bedside showed more autocratic qualities, suggesting that the nearer a nurse leader was to fast-paced clinical demands, the more autocratic they tended to be.

<!--split-->

The main advantage of an autocratic style of leadership is its effectiveness during emergencies. In a code blue, rapid response event, or mass casualty situation, there is no time for group discussion, and one strong voice can save lives. In non-crisis situations, this same quality becomes a hindrance. Reduced trust in management, demotivation of staff members, and feelings of being undervalued or demoralized by exclusion from decisions that affect their work are all qualities associated with sustained autocratic leadership. This can lead to increased staff turnover and reduced morale over time. So autocratic leadership is best applied as a situational management style rather than the norm, used when the need for fast decisions and clarity takes precedence over the value of input and collaboration.

The concept of servant leadership is the opposite of traditional leadership, which centers on the leader's authority and recognition; servant leadership instead looks first at the needs, growth and wellbeing of team members. Nurse leaders who practice this style focus more on listening, empathy and support than on command. A study by Alluhaybi et al. (2023) revealed that servant leadership and the other relational models, transformational, authentic, resonant and ethical, were associated with greater positive nurse engagement practices than distant or directive leadership practices.

Because it builds strong trust and provides support to promote ethical and patient-centered cultures, servant leadership is particularly valuable when mentoring new graduate nurses and combating burnout amongst experienced nurses. It also helps enhance long-term staff retention, as nurses feel genuinely supported. One constraint on servant leadership is speed. Because attending to individual needs and building consensus takes time, this style will not always be feasible; in situations of acute time pressure or chronic understaffing, top-down direction may be needed to help maintain safe and on-time patient care.

<!--split-->

These four styles can be compared to show a consistent tension between speed and collaboration, short-term compliance and long-term engagement. Transformational and servant leadership are gradual processes that take time to establish trust and wellbeing, but they slow down in situations that demand urgency. Transactional and autocratic leadership are quick and structured, but they can lead to disconnection with employees if not balanced with other approaches. However, these styles are not mutually exclusive; based on the positive correlation Moreira et al. (2026) found between transformational and transactional leadership styles, nurse leaders tend to use a combination of approaches as required at any given time. This reflects a situational perspective of leadership that holds there is no single superior method of leadership for everyone. A good nurse leader combines leadership styles, operating in an autocratic mode during crises, using a transactional style for routine compliance, and drawing on a transformational or servant style for morale and retention.

Leadership style in nursing is not a fixed identity but a set of tools that should be matched to the demands of the situation at hand. Transformational leadership fosters trust and wellbeing over time; transactional leadership establishes structure and accountability; autocratic leadership provides direction when time is limited; and servant leadership sustains morale and retention. The sources presented here illustrate that good nurse leaders incorporate a mix of these strategies instead of relying on one approach alone. Education and leadership development programs for nurses should therefore focus on adaptability, helping nursing leaders become familiar with the skills of each approach as needed for different situations. This flexibility has a direct impact on improved patient care, stronger teams, and a healthier nursing workforce.

Nursing Shortage Essay: Causes and Consequences Explained
Nursing Shortage Essay: Causes and Consequences Explained - Essay Example - ThesisArcPro
This nursing shortage essay examines the causes and consequences straining hospitals worldwide, covering burnout, training gaps, and safety risks.

In hospitals worldwide, the same professionals, essential to their operations, are in short supply. The World Health Organization estimates that there will be a shortage of 12.9 million nurses by 2035, putting strain on emergency departments, delaying surgeries, and creating a risk of staff burnout (Tamata & Mohammadnezhad 2023). This nursing shortage is not a quick fix on the staffing front. It stems from a complex mix of workforce failings, nursing education failings and work environment failings and has implications beyond hospital budgets. Patients may wait longer and be at greater risk of medical mistakes, nurses may experience burnout, leading them to leave the profession, and health systems take on the costs of crisis management. However, the nursing shortage is a self-reinforcing process rather than a straightforward supply issue, so each of the causes reinforces the others, and each of the consequences exacerbates the issue of nursing shortage itself. To develop solutions that stick, it's crucial to grasp this cycle, from planning for the workforce to its impact on patients and budgets.

An important factor is the fact that the nursing workforce is aging. Unprepared for the growing complexity of needs among patients, yet nearing retirement age, large numbers of registered nurses are arriving at the same time (Tamata & Mohammadnezhad 2023). Many older nurses are forced into retirement due to the physical strain or a lifetime of years spent in a challenging profession. However, the number of new nurses joining each year has not been commensurate with the number of nurses leaving. In past years, health systems might have been able to replace the loss of senior employees by filling new roles with new hires, but now they are losing key staff at a rate they cannot keep up with. This imbalance of population means the shortage is more than just a blip in the data; if recruitment and retention efforts are not significantly boosted in the near future, it will be a continuing trend.

<!--split-->

Limited capability of nursing education systems to train sufficient numbers of new professionals is the second cause. Even though there are many countries with high demand in nursing schools enrollment, they are short of classroom space, clinical placement sites, and qualified instructors needed to accommodate the high enrollment (Tamata and Mohammadnezhad, 2023). Where areas of interest are not lacking, but rather the institutions themselves are unable to accommodate qualified applicants, the problem is not a lack of interest, but a lack of space. This is a constraint that has repercussions beyond enrollments. Ghimire & Neupane (2024) described how the students of nursing in understaffed clinical situations in Nepal felt abandoned during training, not receiving supervision and mentorship to develop their foundational clinical skills. Others resorted to AI solutions to serve as substitutes for mentoring, a creative and partial solution. It's not just that the professionals are not there to teach the next generation when they are too busy to teach. It compounds and creates less prepared students who are more likely to drop out of school.

Another major culprit, and one of the biggest, is burnout resulting from chronic understaffing. In their review of 33 studies related to the nursing shortage, Jones and Allin (2025) found the most common cause reported in the studies to be stress, burnout, and mental health strain in 18 of the 33 studies, serving as a direct cause of nursing shortages. Nurses who work on a regular basis in understaffed units are carrying more patients, working more hours and have significantly less time to rest and recover. This gradually diminishes nurses' job satisfaction and encourages them to leave the nursing profession, either by leaving their job, transferring to nonclinical positions or by retiring from the profession. The real danger of burnout is that it is both a cause and an effect of the shortage, which is presented in greater detail below.

These combined causes have the most severe impact on the patient. The most common effects reported from hospital nursing shortages, linked to the critical impact of nursing shortages on patient care and safety, are reported in nineteen of the reviewed studies and are followed closely by worsened patient outcomes, in fourteen of the studies. Increased nurse to patient ratios increase the risk of medication not being taken, slow response to complications, and preventable errors. The same issue was explored by Tamata and Mohammadnezhad (2023), who found that the nursing shortage affected early detection of patient complications and thus, overall quality of care. The above are not merely numbers. They are real patients who need enough attentive, well-rested nursing staff at their bedside, something which chronic understaffing makes harder to ensure.

The nursing deficit is a major economic and systemic cost in addition to being a safety concern. In eleven of the studies reviewed in their umbrella review, Jones and Allin (2025) found that reduced system and provider efficiency, such as lost productivity, was cited as a direct impact of hospital nurse shortages. Hospitals with large, persistent staffing deficits may turn to expensive temporary staffing services or overtime to make up for the shortfall, further compressing already limited staffing budgets. Persistent understaffing at smaller or rural facilities may result in staffing reductions and facility closures, potentially affecting access to care for entire communities. Such financial pressures are seldom contained in one hospital. These ripple out and impact insurance costs, public health spending, and the overall ability of health systems to prepare for emergencies or population growth. Loss of local hospital services typically results in increased travel time to access urgent care, particularly affecting rural communities.

Other people believe that technology, such as artificial intelligence and staffing skill mix, can help to solve the nursing problem without an extensive investment in the workforce. Yes, as Ghimire and Neupane (2024) noted, AI-assisted decision support systems have aided students and nurses in navigating information gaps. But nothing will ever replace the clinical judgment, emotional support and mentorship relationships nurses give. Berthelsen and Hansen (2025) concluded that, in their study of nine different introduction programs, the structured and human-led programs all resulted in an increase in retention and a decrease in turnover for newly graduated nurses. This evidence shows that improvements brought about by investing in human-centred solutions rather than the substitution of technologies are measurable and lasting. While technology can help alleviate an over-extended workforce, it can't fix the underlying structural deficiencies that caused the shortage in the first place.

The nursing shortage is a crisis of interlocking causes: an aging nursing workforce, insufficient nursing training and resources, and a nursing workforce experiencing burnout and attrition, with the consequences of that burnout and attrition feeding directly back into the causes of the nursing shortage. Jones and Allin (2025) showed that this feedback loop can cause the shortage to become self-reinforcing, with delayed action causing the problem to worsen rather than improve. Effective solutions must involve policies that increase nursing education capacity, funding for good nursing mentorship, proven policies that retain nurses, and enhanced working conditions to the point that nurses do not prematurely exit. The introduction programs of Berthelsen and Hansen (2025) provide a clear starting point, as they have been shown to measurably increase retention. If the workforce is neglected and not invested in globally, healthcare systems will continue to be squeezed by an ever-increasing shortage of healthcare providers year by year.

Patient-Centered Care: A Nursing Essay Example
Patient-Centered Care: A Nursing Essay Example - Essay Example - ThesisArcPro
This nursing essay example analyzes patient-centered care in nursing, focusing on nurse roles, patient outcomes, and provider barriers today.

Healthcare has been slowly moving from a disease-centric approach to a person-centered one, where the person is the focus of all clinical decisions. This change is because of a growing awareness that a diagnosis is not a treatment for a person. The framework that has emerged to guide this shift is patient-centered care (PCC), which centers on the importance of respect, communication, and shared decision-making with the patient and provider. Nurses, who interact with patients more than any other member of the health care team, are in a unique position to help bring this philosophy into practice. This essay examines essential tenets of patient-centered care, the specialized contribution nurses can make to the delivery of patient-centred care, the evidence to support the connection between patient-centred care and enhanced patient outcomes, and the current challenges impeding the widespread implementation of patient-centred care in healthcare settings. This analysis supports the claim made by recent nursing and public health research that patient-centered care is not just about the bedside manner, but an approach with measurable impacts on the patient and the health system as a whole.

<!--split-->

Patient-centered care is more broadly defined as not just treating the medical condition, but the whole person, including physical, psychological, and social needs. Wasim, Sajan, and Majid (2023) state that researchers and healthcare professionals typically define PCC as both addressing the patient as a whole person and, as a key aspect of PCC, engaging in shared decision making. With the aim of identifying the current status of government-led PCC initiatives in nine developed countries, they conducted an environmental scan of these programs that revealed that, though the concept has been widely adopted, there is no single definition, and its linked relationship with other concepts like patient and family engagement has not been clearly understood. There are significant gaps in the understanding of how to implement PCC programs. This is not a lack of value; it is simply a result of the ambiguity. Instead, it refers to a model where there are consistent values such as respect for patient preferences, coordinating care across the care team, emotional support, clear and honest communication, and continuity of care as the person moves through care settings. These principles are important to have as a foundation for analyzing nursing practice.

Nurses are constantly, directly involved with the patient during an episode of illness and thus are on the frontline of the delivery of patient-centered care. Narayan (2022) carried out in-depth interviews with twenty home health nurses, who expressed that patient-centered care was closely related to being "genuinely invested" in the individual patient, rather than in a case to be managed. Remarkably, the study also found that most of these nurses learned to do things for their patients through trial and error instead of learning it in nursing school or induction programs. This finding is important because it underscores the fact that all the attributes of patient-centered nursing, such as empathy, careful listening, and individualized planning, are learned skills that are not systematically developed. These findings are nuanced by Ferla et al. (2023), who conducted a cross-sectional study of 411 Brazilian health professionals using the Patient-Practitioner Orientation Scale (PPOS). They found that nurses performed moderately well on the caring element of the instrument, but quite poorly on the sharing element, which reflects how much nurses involve patients in decision-making and how much information they share. This gap indicates that nurse-patient relationships are likely strong on the emotional dimension, but that collaborative decision-making may not yet have replaced a more traditional and directive approach, perhaps because of the continuing influence of the biomedical model in nursing education and practice.

<!--split-->

The relationship between patient-centered care and measurable health outcomes has gained increasing attention in nursing and public health studies. Yu et al. (2023) conducted a cross-sectional study of 5,222 inpatients in China to investigate the association between patient-centered care and patients' self-reported physical and mental health status, perceived need for hospitalization, and overutilization of unnecessary services by physicians. They found that the use of more patient-centered practices is linked to improvements in self-reported health and less self-reported unnecessary care. This finding is important because it indicates that the improvement in subjective satisfaction is not a trivial effect of PCC. It appears to affect both the appropriateness of healthcare resource use and patients' own understanding of their illness. The authors also situate their results within a growing body of research suggesting that PCC can help lower information barriers between patients and providers, enabling patients to make more active decisions about their healthcare. But the relationship is not positive in every context. Other studies within the same research literature suggest that PCC effects may not be uniform across all patient populations, and that a single PCC approach might not produce the same result in every clinical setting. This is a key consideration for nurses and healthcare administrators, who must adapt patient-focused practices to account for differences among populations instead of applying a one-size-fits-all model. It also points to the need for more longitudinal studies, since a single cross-sectional survey, no matter how large, cannot fully capture the impact of patient-centered practices on outcomes over time or across repeated hospital visits during a chronic illness.

Although it has many positive aspects, patient-centered care faces several ongoing challenges in nursing practice. One major constraint is time. In the face of heavy workloads, nurses may find it challenging to engage in the kind of conversation that patient-centered care requires, which is deeply personalized and time-consuming. Academic level was also found to be a significant predictor of greater patient-centered attitudes, indicating that further nursing education and specialized training could increase the use of patient-centeredness, but this requires investment that may not always be available to a nursing unit. This concern is supported by the research of Narayan (2022): patient-centered skills are often acquired informally rather than taught formally, resulting in inconsistent practice across the profession. Wasim et al. (2023) also note that cultural sensitivity training is an important but underutilized aspect of patient-centered models, since nurses caring for a multicultural clientele need to be aware of varying cultural expectations regarding communication, autonomy, and family involvement in decision-making. Institutional and systemic resistance also play a role. Time-pressured, efficiency-driven health systems may inadvertently discourage the relationship building that is key to patient-centered care. A challenge that will continue is balancing patient autonomy with clinical guidelines, especially when a patient's preference conflicts with recommended treatment. In these cases, nurses must play a mediating role, conveying clinical reasoning to patients while still respecting their right to make choices about their own treatment.
<!--split-->
Patient-centered care is more than a concept. It is a practical, evidence-based strategy that reshapes how nurses build relationships and share information, and it helps improve patient outcomes. The findings across these four studies are consistent in several ways: nurses play a major role in delivering patient-centered care, that care is evident in some degree of caring behavior, and its presence is measurably linked to both health outcomes and healthcare resource utilization. At the same time, a lack of formal training, inconsistent definitions, and systemic pressures continue to limit how fully this model is implemented in daily practice. Going forward, healthcare systems need to invest more deliberately in teaching patient-centered skills, rather than leaving nurses to learn them through individual experience alone. Doing so would help patient-centered care become a routine practice rather than something that depends on individual effort. The health, safety, and responsiveness of any healthcare system depend on how it treats and cares for the people within it.

Philosophy of Mind Essay: The Mind-Body Problem
Philosophy of Mind Essay: The Mind-Body Problem - Essay Example - ThesisArcPro
This philosophy of mind essay analyzes the mind-body problem through dualism, physicalism, and functionalism, evaluating competing theories of consciousness.

The mind-body problem asks how mental life relates to physical reality. Thoughts, feelings, intentions, perceptions, and conscious experiences appear distinct from measurable brain processes, yet changes to the brain can transform memory, personality, perception, and awareness. The central question is whether subjective consciousness can be fully explained in physical terms alone. Mørch (2023) shows how consciousness poses a genuine challenge to physicalism while surveying the range of non-physicalist alternatives available. This essay argues that dualism captures the distinctive quality of conscious experience, but that its problems with interaction and systematicity weaken its explanatory power. Physicalism and functionalism offer more coherent accounts of how mind depends on and is organized by the body, yet neither adequately explains how physical or computational processes give rise to conscious experience itself.

The gap between mind and body appears in two areas. Physical states are spatial, measurable, and causal; mental states are subjective and carry intentional content. Neural activity can be correlated with pain, for instance, but the felt quality of pain is more than a description of firing neurons. Mørch (2023) identifies this explanatory gap as a central obstacle for physicalism. The difficulty deepens given the apparent causal significance of mental events: decisions give rise to bodily actions, and bodily injuries give rise to conscious pain. Any adequate theory must explain both dependence and difference without resorting to an implausible account of causation. This tension makes consciousness a uniquely demanding test case for any theory that claims to explain the mind purely in terms of physical mechanisms and objective description.

<!--split-->

Substance dualism offers one answer by treating mind and body as two distinct kinds of substance. In the Cartesian tradition, the mind is a thinking, non-extended substance, while the body is physical and extended. Its appeal lies in preserving the distinctiveness of conscious experience rather than reducing thoughts and feelings to purely physical description. As Mørch (2023) explains, the difficulty of accounting for phenomenal consciousness in strictly physical terms continues to motivate theories that are not exclusively physicalist. Dualism therefore takes seriously the intuition that a complete account of physical processes may still fail to capture what an experience feels like from the inside.

Substance dualism, however, faces a well-known problem of interaction. If the mind is non-physical and the body is physical, it is difficult to explain how one could causally affect the other. The close correlation between brain states and mental changes further challenges a theory that separates the two so sharply. Saad (2024) shows that contemporary dualism can be more nuanced than the traditional Cartesian picture; his discussion of "tracking" dualism considers how experiences might relate to physical conditions without assuming an unexplained causal link between two distinct substances. Even so, this refinement does not resolve every difficulty. Saad points to a broader systematicity problem: the question of how psychophysical relations should be structured in a principled way. Dualism offers valuable insight into consciousness, but it commits its defenders to an ambitious theory of the psychophysical connection.

<!--split-->

Physicalism starts from the opposite assumption: that physical reality is all there is, and that mental phenomena must ultimately be explained in physical terms. This view fits naturally with a background in neuroscience, since brain injury, medication, stimulation, and neurological disease can all transform conscious life, suggesting a close relationship between consciousness and physical organization. Mørch (2023) explains that physicalism draws support from this dependence and from causal closure arguments: if physical events already have sufficient physical causes, then adding distinct mental causes seems redundant or creates unwanted competition between causes.

Identity theory offers a stronger version of this idea by equating mental states directly with particular brain states, providing a straightforward account of mental causation. Even so, the problem of phenomenal consciousness remains difficult for physicalists. Explaining neural activity does not, by itself, explain why that processing is accompanied by a subjective point of view. Mørch (2023) raises explanatory, conceivability, and knowledge-based challenges that question whether complete physical knowledge would automatically yield complete knowledge of experience.

Baysan and Wildman (2024) complicate the debate further. Rather than treating physicalism and anti-physicalism as a strict binary, they defend a disjunctive position on which consciousness may be grounded in either physical or non-physical properties depending on the case. Their argument suggests that contemporary philosophy need not force a stark choice between two rigid metaphysical camps. Despite the explanatory strength of physicalism, the metaphysical status of consciousness remains contested because physicalism's explanatory reach still has limits.

<!--split-->

Functionalism offers a third path between substance dualism and strict identity theory. It identifies mental states with their causal and computational roles rather than with any particular material composition, defining a mental state by its inputs, internal interactions, and outputs. On this view, the same type of mental function could, in principle, be realized by different physical systems.

Wiese (2024) examines this question through artificial consciousness and the free energy principle, distinguishing genuine consciousness from processes that merely simulate it. His analysis suggests that reproducing a system's causal organization does not guarantee that the relevant functions, and the experience they might support, are reproduced as well. Wiese's proposed criteria for consciousness emphasize implementation, energy dynamics, causal flow, and existential conditions, with particular weight given to causal organization. This poses a challenge for a purely functionalist approach: matching functional roles may not be sufficient to duplicate consciousness itself. Functionalism improves on strict identity theory by allowing multiple physical realizations of the same mental state, but it still struggles to fully account for subjective experience.

All three approaches illuminate different aspects of the problem. Dualism is strongest in insisting on the apparent irreducibility of subjective experience, but weakest in explaining psychophysical interaction and systematic structure. Physicalism offers the most direct connection to neuroscience by dispensing with any distinct mental substance, yet it faces the explanatory problem of how physical processes could feel like anything from the inside. Functionalism is more flexible than strict identity theory, framing mental states in terms of organization and causal role, but as Wiese (2024) shows, functional or computational similarity alone can still fail to capture genuine consciousness.

The mind-body problem persists because information about brain activity does not amount to information about conscious experience. Substance dualism highlights the distinctive character of mental life, but its problems with interaction and systematicity limit its explanatory power. Physicalism accounts for the mind's dependence on the brain, yet it struggles to explain phenomenal consciousness in purely material terms. Functionalism adds an emphasis on causal organization, though Wiese's analysis shows that computational simulation is not necessarily equivalent to lived experience. Taken together, these four sources suggest that none of these theories fully resolves the problem on its own. The physicalist and functionalist frameworks remain the most coherent available, yet consciousness still points to something that current explanations of brain and behavior have not fully captured.

Police Use of Force Essay: Accountability
Police Use of Force Essay: Accountability - Essay Example - ThesisArcPro
Read this police use of force essay examining police authority, accountability, ethical challenges, and reform through a balanced criminal justice essay.

The use of force by police officers is a topic of significant debate within criminology and law enforcement, impacting public safety, civil liberties, and trust in the police. There are legal reasons for using force when necessary, but there are also many implications to its use that are ethical and legal. In incidents that touch on the question of reasonableness or excessiveness of force, public concern is likely to increase. Policing, on the other hand, is a set of unpredictable encounters that often necessitate officers' quick decision-making in stressful situations. These conflicting realities show that neither totalitarian police nor excessive restrictions has proved itself to be a good solution for society. Rather, effective policing must strike a balance that empowers police officers to intervene in extreme circumstances whilst also ensuring they are held to account via clear oversight, evidence-informed policies, and ongoing professional development.

Police officers are regularly confronted with violent offenders, armed suspects, and individuals with mental health crises. During these interactions, hesitation or poor performance could result in endangering officers and innocent civilians. That's why criminal justice systems acknowledge that officers are entitled to respond with force if and when that is necessary and proportionate to the threat. The use of force continuum is a reflection of this principle, and they should start with verbal and non-violent methods of control, move to less-lethal, and then deadly force only if justified.

The evaluation of police decisions can sometimes be difficult, as officers have limited time to evaluate rapidly changing threats. According to Di Nota et al. (2021), the force evaluation shall take into account objective evidence, as well as subjective human factors such as stress, perception, and cognitive workload. These factors affect officers' perception of danger and reaction to stress. Likewise, Nix (2020) maintains that the context of each use of force incident is unique, as circumstances vary greatly between encounters. Police need to have the necessary powers to safeguard the public. Still, those powers need to be subject to proper and accessible legal frameworks and effective control so that there is no disproportionate or unnecessary use of force.

<!--split-->

Police powers are vital, but so too is accountability when they are not exercised or when they are misused or lack proper review. Low public trust when investigations are inconsistent, disciplinary processes are not transparent, and agencies do not have reliable information on use-of-force incidents. Nix (2020) notes that researchers continue to encounter great challenges given the lack of and inconsistency with national data on police deadly force. If there isn't a standardized reporting system, it is hard for policymakers to identify any trends of misconduct or whether reforms are making a difference.

Lack of accountability systems also makes the organization challenging. DeWitt et al. (2023) list the challenges as a lack of policy consistency, supervision, organizational culture, and transparency. Such weaknesses lead to low levels of public confidence and hinder agencies in their learning from past incidents. In addition, communities may have doubts about the fairness and objectivity of investigations due to inconsistent body camera policies and limited independent oversight. Accountability not only should be a way to tackle misconduct, but also a platform to enhance the legitimacy of law enforcement institutions. Consistency in the behavioral standards of officers helps improve cooperation with police and trust in the justice system.

Practical reforms that will enhance police performance and public trust in the police are essential for effective accountability. There is one key measure that has been promoted as an effective way to increase independent oversight: civilian review boards or external investigative systems. Independent review serves as a way to support the fairness of complaints and minimize perceptions of bias in the investigation.

There is also an important role for technology. Body-worn cameras and clear reporting practices offer important evidence to help with objective analysis of police encounters. Di Nota et al. (2021) suggest that objective measures, like video footage, need to be taken into account with knowledge of officer decision-making to create balanced assessments. These tools help to ensure the safety of officers and the public, and help to document an incident.

Training is yet another critical reform. DeWitt et al. (2023) suggest placing a stronger focus on de-escalation, communication, leadership, and officer wellness to minimize the need for unnecessary force and ensure public safety. Scenario exercises can enhance the ability of officers to make decisions effectively when facing stressful situations and help them defuse violence where possible. Early intervention systems also increase accountability by tracking and flagging problematic behaviors as they occur and before they become a serious disciplinary problem.

Bennell et al. (2021) suggest that police departments need to adopt evidence-based practices that have been substantiated by interdisciplinary research. More interaction between researchers, policies, psychology, and law enforcement professions can lead to better force training, better policies, and more consistent methods of assessing force. These reforms are based on the principle that accountability should be for continuous improvement, not punishment.

Some critics have suggested that more oversight may lead officers to hesitate in making the appropriate decisions in high-risk situations. They argue that their hesitation might result from fear of investigation or, in the event of public criticism, be a risk to officers and civilians. Such concerns should be seriously considered because making decisions under highly stressful situations is often the role performed by police officers.

Effective accountability does not, however, rule out the use of lawful and necessary force by officers. Rather, it sets apart the ethical behavior from the wrong behavior, and it upholds professional ethics. In their article, Di Nota et al. (2021) illustrate how the psychological needs of policing can be used to evaluate the job accurately, instead of criticizing it. In the same way, DeWitt et al. (2023) point out that effective accountability systems promote organizational learning, increase supervision, and boost community trust. Instead of reducing policing, accountability promotes evidence-driven, consistent decision-making that is good for cops and citizens.

The use of force by police will be a key yet highly monitored component of contemporary policing. Police should have enough powers to ensure the safety of communities and deal with unsafe situations, but with clear accountability systems to ensure fairness and trust in the community. Collecting data, providing independent oversight, wearing body cameras, training police, and reforming their practices contribute to better policing. As Nix (2020), Di Nota et al. (2021), DeWitt et al. (2023), and Bennell et al. (2021) all show, authority and accountability are not mutually exclusive aims. They form a criminal justice system that is more effective at ensuring public safety, protecting individual rights, and building trust between police and communities.

Restorative Justice Essay: An Alternative to Incarceration
Restorative Justice Essay: An Alternative to Incarceration - Essay Example - ThesisArcPro
This restorative justice essay analyzes restorative Justice as an alternative to incarceration, emphasizing accountability, rehabilitation, and victim healing.

For many years, the reaction to criminal behavior has focused on punishment, deterrence, and public protection, with justice systems the key focus for decades in response to criminal offending. While imprisonment takes offenders out of society, there are ongoing concerns about the effectiveness of prisons due to overcrowding, a high rate of recidivism, financial costs, and poor rehabilitation. Victim participation and limited opportunity to express the harm they suffered are common in the justice process. Meanwhile, criminals can walk out of prison without dealing with the root causes of their crimes. The above limitations have prompted researchers and practitioners to seek a complementary and alternative approach to crime: restorative Justice. Restorative Justice is a process that focuses on the repair of the harm, rather than punishment, through dialogue, accountability, and community involvement. It does not just punish for illegal activities but attempts to repair any harmed or broken relationships that occurred as a result of illegal acts. This essay suggests that restorative Justice offers a valuable alternative to imprisonment as a means of making offenders accountable, involving victims in the process, offering chances for offenders to be treated as people who need to be helped, and holding communities accountable. This is the power of restorative Justice, but it requires careful application, especially when it comes to serious violent crime.

Restorative Justice is a philosophy and group of practices that aims to restore the harm that has been caused by criminal behavior, and to engage with parties to the conflict, including victims, offenders, and communities, actively. Gade (2021) notes that restorative Justice is fundamentally different from punishment in that it is not about causing suffering but about restoring broken relationships and getting offenders to make serious amends for their actions. Crime is thus seen not just as an infringement on the law, but as an assault on people and communities, causing harm and thus deserving of repair.

Examples of restorative practices include, among others, victim-offender mediation, family group conferencing, and restorative circles. The strategies provide a framework for victims to share the emotional, financial, and social impact of crime and for offenders to accept responsibility in a direct way and enter into agreements for rectifying the harm. Community members are regularly involved, supporting reconciliation and effective reintegration. The concept of accountability is more than just facing punishment (Gade, 2021): the offender also has to be responsible for making amends for what they did wrong. Restorative Justice, therefore, helps to encourage dialogue, empathy, responsibility, and a focus on both parties, not just one.

<!--split-->

Although it serves a crucial function in the protection of society from dangerous offenders, incarceration has some serious drawbacks when it is the primary method of criminal Justice. Traditional prison sentences often focus on punishment, neglecting to offer the necessary opportunities for rehabilitation, education, or psychological care. As a result, a significant number of offenders re-enter the community without developing the skills and behavior change to prevent reoffending.

In Forsberg and Douglas (2022), the authors state that rehabilitation is one of the "focal points" of the criminal justice system as it seeks to restore the capacity of the offender to live lawfully. Punishment is not effective at this goal – behavior change must also include change, or affect personal situations, attitudes, and decision making. Incarceration can postpone, not prevent, future crime if the person is not suitably rehabilitated.

Traditional justice systems also offer relatively little opportunity to victims beyond giving evidence to engage in the justice process. The focus of criminal proceedings is on guilt and punishment, leaving many victims in emotional turmoil even years later. Communities also face high financial and social costs because of the imprisonment of their citizens, such as income loss for former prisoners, the cost of corrections, and disruptions to families. The challenges are evidence that alternatives are needed that are focused on rehabilitation.

Many of the failures of incarceration are addressed directly in restorative Justice, particularly in the context of holding people accountable, healing harms, and repairing damage. In place of being punished as victims, restorative programs require offenders to face the implications of what they've done, accept responsibility, and engage in active participation in making amends. This process helps to foster a culture of Justice and accountability by helping offenders understand the consequences of their actions on others and communities. Gade (2021) says that restorative dialogue helps offenders understand the emotional, social, and financial impact on the victim, fostering opportunities for real reconciliation. Victim(s) have the opportunity to share their story, ask questions, and participate in determining what would happen. This involvement can foster healing and enhance satisfaction with the justice process.

These benefits are also confirmed by empirical evidence. Within prisons, Peleg-Koriat et al. (2025) concluded that victim awareness training programs had a significant impact on enhancing offenders' empathy, acceptance of personal responsibility, and support for restorative practices. Should Healthcare Be a Fundamental Right?
Healthcare as a Fundamental Right Essay - Essay Example - ThesisArcPro
Explore whether healthcare should be a fundamental right guaranteed by the government, focusing on dignity, universal access, and economic benefits.

Healthcare is one of the most basic human needs, yet millions of people around the world lack access to appropriate medical services. The question of whether healthcare should be a fundamental right guaranteed by government continues to shape policy debates worldwide, touching on how societies balance individual responsibility, collective welfare, and the role of the state. While several countries still treat healthcare as a product available only to those who can afford it, the ethical, economic, and social implications of that approach deserve careful attention. Healthcare must be regarded as a human right and provided by the state, because access to medical care is central to human dignity, universal coverage produces healthier and more productive communities, and publicly funded systems save money compared to profit-oriented medicine. Treating healthcare as a commodity rather than a right leaves outcomes contingent on employment status, income, and geography, factors that have little to do with medical need and everything to do with circumstance.

<!--split-->

Access to healthcare largely determines human dignity and equality in contemporary society. Healthcare is not only about treating illness; it shapes a person's ability to live a full life, participate in the workforce, and remain an active member of society. Without guaranteed healthcare, vulnerable groups such as the poor, the elderly, and the chronically ill are left without access to basic services, often suffering avoidable pain and dying prematurely. This marginalization deepens social inequality and reinforces cycles of poverty, since illness and financial hardship tend to compound one another over time. In a fair society, a person's right to healthcare should not depend on their financial means. Galvani-Townsend et al. (2022) find that mean life expectancy in countries with publicly funded healthcare systems is 76.7 years, compared to 66.8 years in countries without such systems, a gap of roughly a decade that reveals the dramatic effect access to healthcare has on human lifespan. This pattern holds even in countries facing a high burden of adverse social determinants, where publicly funded healthcare continues to raise life expectancy across nearly every socioeconomic level despite challenging economic and social conditions (Galvani-Townsend et al., 2022). These findings point to both a moral obligation and a practical case for ensuring vulnerable populations have access to the care they need, rather than leaving basic survival contingent on income. Framing healthcare in terms of dignity also shifts the policy conversation away from questions of individual deservingness and toward a shared baseline of care that every person can expect regardless of circumstance.

This same emphasis on human dignity is reflected in the outcomes of countries that have implemented universal healthcare. Developed nations such as the United Kingdom, Canada, and Japan report higher life expectancy and lower infant mortality than countries without universal coverage. Universal healthcare systems also make preventive care more accessible, which is critical for reducing the long-term costs associated with treating advanced disease once it has progressed beyond early, manageable stages. The improved outcomes that come from early treatment, paired with freedom from the fear of financial ruin due to illness, add up to better health across the population as a whole. The evolution of Universal Health Coverage through the Primary Health Care era (1978–2000), the Millennium Development Goals (2000–2015), and the current Sustainable Development Goals (2015–2030) has coincided with rising average life expectancy, significant declines in maternal and child mortality, sharply reduced severe malnutrition in most regions, and high immunization rates against major infectious diseases (Ranabhat et al., 2023). This historical trend suggests that sustained investment in universal coverage meaningfully improves population health over time, rather than producing only short-term or isolated gains. Universal Health Coverage first took shape during the Primary Health Care period, which emphasized community involvement and equitable access, later extending to broader immunization and disease-prevention programs that reached populations previously excluded from formal medical systems.

<!--split-->

Beyond these health outcomes, a closer economic examination shows that state-supplied healthcare offers clearer financial advantages than private alternatives. Pharmaceutical companies and private insurers operate on a profit motive that tends to push healthcare costs upward, since pricing decisions are shaped as much by shareholder returns as by patient need. Publicly funded systems, by contrast, can negotiate lower prices for medication and care, reducing overall costs and spreading financial risk across the entire population, which makes healthcare both more affordable and more accessible, including for those most economically at risk. In a systematic review of 22 economic analyses of single-payer healthcare systems, Cai et al. (2020) found that 19 studies, or 86 percent, projected net savings within the first year, with median first-year savings of 3.46 percent of total healthcare expenditure, while 20 studies, or 91 percent, projected net savings over multiple years as compounding growth continued. The largest share of these savings came from simplified payment administration, with median savings of 8.8 percent, while drug-cost savings were the strongest predictor of overall net savings in the multivariate analysis (Cai et al., 2020). The negotiating power of the U.S. Veterans Administration, which secures roughly 30 percent discounts on prescription drugs compared with private Medicare Advantage plans, further illustrates how government-run healthcare systems can be both more equitable and more cost-effective (Cai et al., 2020). Together, these findings show that government-regulated systems tend to reduce administrative costs and negotiate lower healthcare prices, producing benefits that extend across society rather than concentrating gains among shareholders or high-income patients.

Critics acknowledge that healthcare access matters for human dignity and equality, that universal systems improve public health outcomes and generate economic benefits, and that government-provided healthcare tends to be more affordable and equitable than private care, yet they still raise concerns worth addressing directly rather than dismissing outright. Wait times for non-emergency services can be longer in some countries with universal coverage, but overall health outcomes remain considerably better than in countries without such systems. As Galvani-Townsend et al. (2022) show, publicly funded healthcare is consistently associated with longer life expectancy across every level of social determinants, with life expectancy ranging from 68.12 to 80.88 years across performance quartiles in countries with public funding, compared with 62.39 to 77.33 years in countries without it. Countries with Universal Health Coverage have found ways to allocate resources effectively through context-specific reforms, including the health transformation plans in Iran and Turkey, health system reform in Mexico, and expanded health insurance in the Republic of Korea, offering practical models for other countries pursuing universal coverage (Ranabhat et al., 2023). These systems generally place greater emphasis on preventive care and early intervention, which reduces the need for costly late-stage treatment and improves population-wide health outcomes over the long run. Rather than treating longer wait times as evidence against universal systems, this comparison suggests they are better understood as a manageable trade-off against far larger, population-wide gains in health and longevity.

<!--split-->

The claim of inefficiency does not hold up well under scrutiny when overall cost-effectiveness is considered rather than isolated line items. Cai et al. (2020) find broad consensus across studies that the efficiency savings of single-payer systems outweigh any added costs. Average net savings of 3 to 4 percent in the first year, growing at roughly 1.4 percent annually thereafter, suggest that even the small number of studies projecting first-year net costs still anticipate net savings within a decade. These savings can be redirected toward improving quality and expanding access to care, directly addressing efficiency concerns rather than simply cutting services (Cai et al., 2020). Realizing this potential requires implementation strategies that simplify payment administration in line with other countries, negotiate significantly lower drug prices, and use clinical data to identify and reduce unnecessary or unwarranted care, so that savings translate into better outcomes rather than disappearing into administrative overhead.

Healthcare should be treated as an essential human right and provided by government. Universal access supports human dignity and equality, produces better health outcomes, and generates significant economic advantages. Publicly funded healthcare systems demonstrate greater cost-efficiency and equity than privately run systems, since removing the profit motive allows access to care regardless of income. While critics argue that such systems introduce inefficiencies, the experience of countries with successful universal healthcare shows these systems tend to be more sustainable, more equitable, and produce better health outcomes overall. Ensuring healthcare is treated as a universal right ultimately serves society's broader interest: when everyone can access the care they need, communities become healthier, more productive, and fairer as a result.

Should the Majority Always Decide What Is Good?
Should the Majority Always Decide What Is Good? - Essay Example - ThesisArcPro
A critical analysis of utilitarianism, examining why majority rule alone is insufficient for determining the greatest ethical good in society.

Utilitarianism is a form of consequentialist ethical thought that asserts that actions ought to maximize the amount of happiness and well-being for the greatest number of people. This seemingly straightforward principle has been used as a guide for moral decision-making for centuries, in fields such as healthcare, public policy, and social welfare. However, there is a fundamental problem when putting utilitarian ethics into practice: who is to determine what constitutes the "greatest good"? If we default to majority preferences by default, then we risk justifying the oppression of minorities and missing important considerations about human flourishing. The purpose of this analysis is to discuss the shortcomings of majority rule in establishing ethical outcomes by examining recent scholarship of the utilitarian system as well as comparative systems of ethics. This essay argues that while utilitarianism offers sound principles for the greatest possible collective welfare, the greater good should not be unilaterally decided upon by the majority because the act ignores the rights of the minority, does not take into consideration the quality of preferences, and does not acknowledge the need for expert moral reasoning in critical ethical conditions.

<!--split-->
** The Problem of Minority Rights and Majority Tyranny**

Allowing majority rule to decide what the most excellent good is runs significant risks to vulnerable populations and minority groups. When utilitarian calculations aggregate the preferences of the majority, grave harms to outgroup members may be justified. Morrell & Dahlmann (2022) agree that utilitarian frameworks often get lost in debates over protecting individual rights when collective calculations favor the majority, creating systematic vulnerabilities for marginalized populations. This weakness is seen in health care rationing, resource allocation, and policy decisions where the preferences of the majority often supersede the demands of minority interests. Wesseh (2025) argues that deontological ethics provides stronger protections against such majoritarianism by setting inviolable duties that consequential calculations cannot outweigh. Even when the majority truly believes their preferences are in the best interest of all, they may lack the knowledge of minority experiences and needs. The modern utilitarian theory needs to incorporate limits on rights to avoid the oppression of vulnerable populations (Häyry, 2021). Methods of ensuring the interests of minorities must entail more than the aggregation of their preferences, e.g., the means to protect from majoritarian oppression, irrespective of utilitarian calculations.

** The Quality and Complexity of Moral Preferences**

Not all preferences count equally in genuine human flourishing, and thus, mere counting of the majority is not enough in determining the greatest good. People tend to prioritize immediate rewards over long-term health, opt for what they already know over what's objectively better, or endorse policies based on misinformation rather than evidence. Häyry (2021) shows that reformulations of utilitarian theory increasingly embody more nuanced conceptualizations of well-being that remain independent of preferences and focus on objective conditions of human flourishing rather than on subjective preferences. The subjectivist approach recognizes that majorities can be wrong about what maximizes welfare — especially if they know insufficient facts or have no facts about the issue. Social welfare functions must be designed to take into account how preferences are formulated and whether they actually capture individual and collective welfare (Karami, 2024). And beyond that, preferences are influenced by social conditioning, the uneven distribution of wealth, and power structures that may bias people about what they think is in their best interest. Bostyn et al. (2023) noted that moral judgments are often influenced by cognitive biases and social factors rather than the rational assessment of outcomes. Thus, the greatest good must be discovered by a careful examination of what most determines human flourishing, rather than mindlessly deferring to the opinion of the majority.

** The Necessity of Moral Expertise and Reasoned Judgment**

Ethical decision-making involves special knowledge and careful reasoning and is free of popular opinion or majority vote. Complex moral questions involve empirical facts about human psychology, social consequences, and long-term effects, which most people lack the expertise to address thoroughly. Karami (2024) examines the passage of utilitarian social welfare functions requiring sophisticated analysis of impact on different populations and demonstrates that deciding acceptable policy outcomes involves the use of rigorous methodology as opposed to intuitive judgment. Professional ethicists, social scientists, and members of the affected communities have valuable insights that should factor into utilitarian calculations rather than being overruled by uninformed majority opinion. Transitioning from NICU to Family Nurse Practitioner
Transitioning from NICU to Family Nurse Practitioner - Essay Example - ThesisArcPro
This essay discusses the transition from NICU and pediatric nursing to Family Nurse Practitioner, reflecting on skills gained along the way.

Hello, ladies and gentlemen, welcome to this forum!

From my experience, I have realized that transitioning from the NICU, postpartum, and pediatric care to Family Nurse Practitioner (FNP) is a momentous experience in my career growth. Having worked in various settings, I possess strong, insightful skills in primary care to save patients' lives. I have worked in both flexible and strict environments, which has given me an understanding of different work conditions in both child- and adult-based settings.

<!--split-->

During my shift, one of the key adjustments I made was advancing towards preventive care and disease management. These roles are complex and require clinical commitment, ethics, and compassion in serving patients. Since the environment is engaging, you are expected to expand your hourly vitals and focus on complex scenarios for longer periods (Hoffman et al., 2026). In this case, a nurse is expected to partner with patients in clinical decision-making and solving health issues. In the NICU, a nurse focuses on less complex pediatric care. In contrast, in the client-nurse partnership, an FNP's role is demanding and requires autonomy in patient care and in offering medical solutions.

In FNP, nurse roles are advanced and require autonomy to cope with patient health patterns. In addressing health issues, several primary care skills are needed to ensure quality care. One key aspect is comprehensive wellness child care. It involves understanding analytics, growth charts, and developmental milestones (Hoffman et al., 2026). Understanding pediatric health patterns allows health nurses to manage pediatric conditions and improve clinical outcomes. Secondly, a nurse needs postpartum continuity skills (Hoffman et al., 2026). This involves skills needed to address complex conditions such as cardiovascular conditions, preeclampsia, and others. Addressing primary concerns helps achieve high-quality health outcomes for patients. Thirdly, one needs family education (Hoffman et al., 2026). Since the pediatric environment involves working with parents and families facing emotional challenges, it is important to learn how to comfort and guide them in handling challenging health outcomes.
<!--split-->

In conclusion, having a specialty in the NICU provides a foundational background for family practice. Shifting from child care to lifespan-focused care allows one to enhance skills in disease management. To cope with changing career expectations, a nurse is expected to develop diagnostic intuition, deepen knowledge in family education, and focus on effective communication and interactions with families in times of grief. With these skills, your unique career perspective will heavily contribute to professionalism and understanding clinical dynamics.

## References
